column4: The Messenger brings light and a clear Book, making clear much of what Scripture holders had concealed. This directly develops the source section’s passage from hidden teaching to explanation and public disclosure.

The verse calls the sent-down Book a clarification for all things and guidance. This directly parallels the source section’s dictionary sense of ش ر ح as making something clear, now stated as the Book’s purpose.

The Prophet is told to recite what has been revealed from his Lord’s Book, whose words cannot be altered. This joins the source section’s Qur’an-on-the-tongue image to the preservation of the recited text.
The verse calls the reminder for the Prophet’s generation and for those before them. It directly supports the source section’s dictionary claim that the books of earlier prophets are dhikr as well.

The verse says the Word has been conveyed to the people so that they may remember. It directly meets the source section’s account of a word spread outward and dhikr as what brings something back to mind.

The verse asks whether it is not enough that the Book was sent down and is recited to them, and calls it mercy and reminder for believers. It concretely joins the source section’s Book-as-dhikr to public recitation.

The Prophet is not taught poetry; the revelation is a reminder and a clear Qur’an. This specifies the source section’s spoken dhikr as clear revealed speech, and distinguishes it from another kind of utterance.
The verse says there is a reminder for one who has a heart or gives ear while present. This connects the source section’s memory held in the heart with its spoken word that reaches a listener.
The verse says the Merciful taught al-bayān. The source section explicitly gives al-bayān as the dictionary wording for ش ر ح; this ayah names that clarifying expression as something taught.
The ayah says a reminder may benefit its hearer. It directly matches the source section’s dictionary definition of tadhkira as what enables remembering.
A group of jinn listen to the Qur’an, then return to their people as warners. This concretely stages the source section’s word carried aloud and disseminated from one audience to another.

The next ayah reports the jinn identifying what they heard as a Book sent down after Moses and guiding to truth. Its own contribution is to name the heard recitation as scripture, matching the source section’s prophetic-book sense of dhikr.
The jinn then urge their people to answer God’s caller and believe. This completes the transmission begun in 46:29–30 with the response sought from those who hear the message.
A group of jinn hear the recitation and repeat that they have heard a wondrous Qur’an. This directly stages the source section’s spoken word becoming something an audience remembers and reports.

The next ayah says that the Qur’an guides to the right way and that the listeners believe in it. It gives the response to the hearing scene in 72:1, showing the public recitation retained as guidance.
The Qur’an is described as a reminder for those who fear. This is a direct instance of the source section’s dictionary sense of prophetic scripture as dhikr.
The verse says people of God should teach the Book and study it. This is a specific practice of keeping and transmitting scripture, though it does not use the source section’s word dhikr.

The signs are explained in varied ways so that the message may be made clear to people who know. This parallels the source section’s movement from what is closed to what is explained, though the ayah does not use the root ش ر ح.

This Qur’an relates to the Children of Israel much of what they differ about. That gives a specific interpretive parallel to the source section’s dictionary sense of ش ر ح as explanation, although this ayah says it recounts rather than using the source term.
The Merciful is said to have taught the Qur’an. This is a specific instance of the prophetic Book as taught discourse, corresponding to the source section’s dictionary sense of dhikr as scripture.
The successful person remembers the name of his Lord and prays. This is a concrete instance of the source section’s ذ ك ر as keeping a thing in mind and letting it be present in utterance.
The opening command is to read in the name of the Lord. This gives a specific recitation scene for the source section’s image of a reader bearing Qur’an on the tongue.

A group hear God’s words and then deliberately distort them after understanding. This is a specific reversal of the source section’s preserved and clarified word: hearing and carrying revelation can also be followed by deliberate alteration.

Some twist their tongues with the Book so listeners think their speech belongs to Scripture, though it does not. This is a concrete misuse of the source section’s tongue-carried Book image, false public transmission rather than faithful recitation.
The ayah says God taught by the pen. Alongside the reading command in 96:1, it supplies the written side of the source section’s paired images of remembered scripture and Qur’an carried in speech.
